1359.title: The Divine Liturgy
1359.hook: the liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, sung almost entirely
1359.howItsDone: Byzantine Catholics, like Orthodox Christians, celebrate the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom on most Sundays; it is sung throughout, with the people or a choir answering the priest and deacon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Byzantine churches: Catholics who share their worship with the Orthodox. Your line was east in communion.

An old chronicle of Kyiv tells a story about where the faith of its people began. Their prince, the story goes, sent envoys to see how other peoples worshiped. In Constantinople they were taken into the great church of Holy Wisdom on a feast day. Lamps. Gold. Incense rising. Voices answering each other across the church. Back home, the chronicle says, their report was simple: they didn't know whether they had been in heaven or on earth. They only knew that God dwelt there among people. It's a story, told long after. But it names what the liturgy itself is reaching for.
screen: `ENVOYS FROM KYIV.` → `THE CHURCH OF HOLY WISDOM.` → `HEAVEN OR EARTH?`

segments.voice: First, the name. In the Byzantine churches, Catholic and Orthodox, the usual Sunday service is the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom, a bishop of Constantinople remembered for his preaching. Chrysostom was a nickname: golden-mouthed. It's the Byzantine Mass, the same Eucharist, the same bread and wine, in another shape. Second, the singing. Almost nothing in it is simply spoken. The priest sings, the deacon sings, and the people or the choir sing back. The deacon calls out petitions, for peace, for the sick, for travelers, for the city, and after each one comes the answer: Lord, have mercy. Again and again, like waves. Third, the Cherubic Hymn. As the bread and wine are carried in procession, the choir sings that the people, in a mystery, stand in for the cherubim, the angels around God's throne, and asks them to lay aside all earthly cares to receive the King of all. Fourth, the angels' song. Later the people sing the song Isaiah heard in his vision, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." The Latin Mass sings it too. And the Second Vatican Council taught that the earthly liturgy is a foretaste of the liturgy of heaven, joined to it. That's what the envoys were trying to say: in the Divine Liturgy, earth borrows heaven's song for a while, and the bills and the group chats wait outside.

1360.title: The iconostasis
1360.hook: a wall of icons between the nave and the altar
1360.howItsDone: In Byzantine churches, Catholic and Orthodox, the iconostasis separates the nave from the sanctuary; people venerate its icons with a bow, the sign of the cross, a kiss or a candle, and the doors open at set moments of the liturgy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Divine Liturgy: sung almost from start to finish, with earthly cares left at the door. Your line was heaven on earth.

From the back of a Byzantine church, you can barely see the altar. What you see is a wall: a screen of wood or stone running the width of the church, covered in painted faces on gold. Saints. Angels. A mother and child. A man with a long beard holding a scroll. Their eyes look straight out. In the middle there are doors, and during the liturgy they open, a deacon comes through with incense, and for a moment you glimpse the altar behind. Then the doors close, and the faces are watching again.
screen: `A WALL OF PAINTED FACES.` → `DOORS IN THE MIDDLE.` → `THE ALTAR, GLIMPSED.`

segments.voice: You met John of Damascus and the icons earlier on this path. First, what it is. The iconostasis stands between the nave, where the people pray, and the sanctuary, where the altar is. It has a central pair of doors, the Royal or Holy Doors, and usually a smaller door on each side, for the deacons. Second, the order of it. To the right of the central doors, as you face it, is Christ; to the left, his mother, holding him. Next to them often stand John the Baptist and the saint the church is named for, and in larger churches, rows above them: the great feasts, the apostles, the prophets. The whole story of salvation on one screen. Third, why paint God at all. Paul writes of Christ, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is the image of the invisible God." The Greek word for image there is eikon, icon. Because God became flesh and could be seen, Catholics and Orthodox alike hold that he can be painted. The Second Council of Nicaea taught that the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows. Nobody here is praying to wood. Fourth, a window, not a wall. It looks like a barrier. But its faces are the ones Hebrews calls "so great a cloud of witnesses." They're not keeping you out; they're showing you who's already inside, and when the doors open, the Church can see straight through to the altar. The room is full before anyone gets there.

1361.title: Babies receive everything
1361.hook: in the East, infants are baptized, chrismated and given communion together
1361.howItsDone: In Eastern Catholic and Orthodox churches, an infant is baptized by triple immersion, chrismated with holy myron, and given communion from a spoon, usually in one celebration; Latin Catholics baptize infants and celebrate first communion and confirmation in later years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the iconostasis: a wall of faces that turns out to be a window. Your line was the icon screen.

The baby does not approve. She's been lowered into the warm water of the font three times, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and she's letting the whole church know about it. Then, still damp and wrapped in a towel, she's anointed with holy oil: forehead, eyes, nose, mouth, ears, chest, hands, feet. And later, when the people come forward for communion, the priest lifts a small spoon to her mouth, a tiny portion of the consecrated wine. Baptized. Sealed with the Spirit. Fed at the altar. All before she can say a single word.
screen: `THREE TIMES INTO THE WATER.` → `ANOINTED WITH HOLY OIL.` → `A SPOON AT THE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: First, the three. Catholics call baptism, confirmation and the Eucharist the sacraments of initiation: the way someone is brought all the way into the Church. The Catechism says plainly that in the Eastern rites, the initiation of infants begins with baptism, followed immediately by confirmation and the Eucharist. In the East, confirmation is called chrismation, and the priest anoints with the words: the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Second, the West spreads them out. In the Latin Church, babies are baptized, and then come years of learning before first communion and confirmation later on. The Catechism holds the two side by side and ranks neither: the Eastern way shows the unity of the three sacraments; the Latin way, by keeping confirmation with the bishop, shows the bond with him. Same three gifts, different timing. Third, the reason the Catechism gives. When it describes the Eastern churches giving communion to the newly baptized, even little children, it recalls the Lord's words, in the Douay-Rheims: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not." Fourth, grace before understanding. A baby understands none of it. Doesn't know the creed, can't say amen, can't even hold her head up. That's the point both East and West make by baptizing infants at all: grace is a gift, not a prize. The East simply carries that logic all the way to the table.

1362.title: Married priests
1362.hook: Eastern Catholic priests are often married
1362.howItsDone: In the Eastern Catholic churches married men may be ordained deacons and priests, provided they marry before ordination; bishops are chosen from celibate clergy. In the Latin Church, priests are normally celibate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, babies receive everything: in the Eastern churches an infant is baptized, chrismated and given communion in one morning. Your line was all three at once.

Sunday, after the Divine Liturgy, in a parish hall that smells of coffee. The priest is still in his black cassock, and a small boy is tugging at its hem, asking for a donut. His own son. Across the room a woman pours coffee and greets newcomers by name, and people call her by a title of her own. For a Latin Catholic visiting for the first time, it's a double take. A married Catholic priest? Nobody here is breaking a rule. This is an Eastern Catholic parish, in full communion with Rome, doing what its tradition has long done.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH A SON AT HIS HEM.` → `A WOMAN WITH A TITLE OF HER OWN.` → `NOBODY IS BREAKING A RULE.`

segments.voice: The New Testament doesn't hide that the apostles had families. Mark's Gospel says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Simon's wife's mother lay in a fit of a fever," and Jesus heals her. Simon is Peter. Peter had a mother-in-law, so Peter had a wife. And when Paul lists what a bishop should be, he writes that he must be "blameless, the husband of one wife." Today the Catechism sets two disciplines side by side. In the Latin Church, priests are normally chosen from men who live a celibate life and intend to keep it, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. In the Eastern Churches a different discipline has been in force for many centuries: bishops are chosen only from celibates, but married men can be ordained deacons and priests. Both, the Catechism says, are honored. Neither is called second best. The order of things surprises people. A man marries first, and then may be ordained. A priest doesn't go looking for a wife after ordination; if a single man is ordained, he stays single. And the woman at the coffee urn? Her life is shaped by her husband's calling too: the late phone calls, the shared table, the move to a new parish. Greek speakers call her presbytera. In Arabic-speaking parishes she is khouria. Ukrainians have their own word for her, and so do Russians. Her title is spoken with respect.

1363.title: The Maronites
1363.hook: Lebanon's Syriac church, which says it never broke communion with Rome
1363.howItsDone: Maronite Catholics celebrate the Qurbono, their Divine Liturgy, in the West Syriac tradition, with parts in Syriac and the rest in Arabic or the local language; they honor Saint Maron and Saint Charbel, and their parishes stand in countries far from Lebanon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, married priests: an Eastern man may marry and then be ordained, and his wife has a title of her own. Your line was the priest's wife.

A flag with a green tree in the middle. That's the flag of Lebanon, and the tree is a cedar. Walk into a Maronite church, in Beirut or in a suburb far from the Mediterranean, and listen. The priest prays some of the words of consecration in Syriac, a language close to the one Jesus spoke, and the people answer, often in Arabic. A family that's been in that parish for generations will tell you something they're proud of: their church says it never broke communion with Rome. Not reunited. Never left.
screen: `A CEDAR ON A FLAG.` → `PRAYERS IN SYRIAC.` → `NOT REUNITED. NEVER LEFT.`

segments.voice: The name comes from Saint Maron, a hermit who, tradition says, lived his prayer out in the open air on a hillside in Syria and drew disciples around him. Monks who followed his way became the heart of a church. Over time, the story goes, that community found its home in the mountains of Lebanon, where steep valleys sheltered monasteries and villages. Then the claim. Some Eastern Catholic churches tell of a moment when a community, once separated, came into communion with Rome. Maronites tell their story differently: there was no such moment, because there was no break. Historians discuss the details; the Maronite church holds this as part of who it is. The Bible loves Lebanon's cedars. Psalm ninety-one in the Douay-Rheims says, "The just shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow up like the cedar of Libanus." Libanus is Lebanon. A cedar grows slowly, lives long, smells of resin, and holds its ground on a mountainside. Maronites have taken it as a picture of their own faith: rooted, patient, hard to uproot. Last, a saint who fits the tree. Saint Charbel was a Maronite monk who spent his last years as a hermit in the mountains, praying in silence, and pilgrims still climb to his monastery. The church that began with a hermit on a hillside keeps producing hermits on hillsides. And wherever Maronite families have moved, they've carried the cedar with them, sometimes literally, painted over the church door.

1364.title: The Thomas Christians
1364.hook: the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara churches of India trace their faith to Thomas
1364.howItsDone: Syro-Malabar Catholics celebrate the Holy Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition and Syro-Malankara Catholics in the West Syriac tradition, mostly in Malayalam; both churches honor Saint Thomas as the apostle who, by their tradition, brought the faith to India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maronites: a church of Lebanon, named for a hermit, that says it never left communion with Rome. Your line was the cedars.

Kerala, on the southwest coast of India. Coconut palms, backwaters, rain that arrives like a wall. A bride in a gold-bordered sari walks out of a church, and her family has kept the faith for as long as anyone can say. Ask them where it came from, and they won't say Portugal, or England, or a missionary from Europe. They'll name an apostle. Thomas, they'll tell you. He came here. Some of their churches carry his name over the door. Today, the people who call themselves his children.
screen: `A WEDDING IN KERALA.` → `NOT EUROPE. AN APOSTLE.` → `THOMAS, THEY SAY.`

segments.voice: The Gospels show Thomas as more than a doubter. When Jesus decides to go back toward danger in Judea, John's Gospel gives Thomas the brave line: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Later, yes, he says he won't believe the resurrection until he touches the wounds. But when he sees Jesus, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "My Lord, and my God." Bold, then doubting, then a confession that calls Jesus Lord and God. Then India. The Gospels end before Thomas's travels begin. Ancient tradition says he sailed east and preached on the Malabar coast, and the Christians of Kerala keep that memory, with places and songs tied to his name. Scholars debate the history; the families don't need them to settle it to know who they are. Today two Eastern Catholic churches belong to this family. The Syro-Malabar Church prays in the East Syriac tradition, the Syro-Malankara Church in the West Syriac tradition, and both call their Eucharist the Holy Qurbana. Not every Thomas Christian is Catholic: Orthodox and other churches share the same heritage, and the same apostle. What they've kept is a faith fully Indian, at home in a land of many faiths, with customs drawn from their own soil, and fully Catholic too. The faith wasn't imported, they'd say. It grew here, from a seed an apostle planted.

1365.title: The Chaldeans
1365.hook: Iraq's Catholics still pray in a form of Aramaic; Francis visited them in 2021
1365.howItsDone: Chaldean Catholics celebrate the Holy Qurbana in the East Syriac tradition, praying in Syriac and Arabic and, abroad, in local languages; their patriarch is based in Baghdad, and Chaldean parishes abroad serve families who left Iraq.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Thomas Christians of India, who name an apostle as the one who brought them the faith. Your line was thomas's children.

"Talitha cumi." Jesus takes a dead girl by the hand and says those words, and she gets up. Mark's Gospel sets them down as they sounded, then translates: damsel, arise. He leaves the words standing, like stones in a field, so a reader hears the voice. Readers take them as Aramaic, the speech of Jesus's world. Now go to a village church on the plain near Mosul, in northern Iraq, or a church in Baghdad. On Sunday, priest and people pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic: words from the same family as talitha cumi, still in the mouths of a living congregation.
screen: `TALITHA CUMI.` → `ARAMAIC LEFT STANDING IN MARK.` → `STILL PRAYED IN IRAQ.`

segments.voice: The name reaches back to Abraham. Genesis says his family set out from Ur of the Chaldeans, and the Chaldean Catholic Church takes its name from that old region, in what is now Iraq. Its people speak of themselves as heirs of some of the earliest Christian communities of Mesopotamia. Then the language. Mark keeps Aramaic more than once. On the cross, he writes, Jesus cried, "Eloi, Eloi, lamma sabacthani?" and then translates it: my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Syriac, the language of the Chaldean liturgy, is a form of Aramaic, written in its own script. When Chaldeans pray the Our Father in Syriac, the sound is a near neighbor of the sound in that Galilean house. Then the hard years. Iraq's Christians have lived through war, and in recent years families fled when an extremist group overran their towns on the Nineveh Plain. Churches were burned. Some families came back to rebuild; others now pray in Syriac far from home. And then a visit. Pope Francis traveled to Iraq, prayed among the ruins of Mosul's churches, and went to Ur, the place of Abraham, to pray with Muslims, Yazidis and others who honor Abraham too. Look back at this week: a Divine Liturgy sung almost entirely, a wall of icons, a baby given everything at once, a priest's wife with a title, cedars in Lebanon, Thomas's children in India, and now Chaldeans in Iraq. One Catholic Church, many ancient homes.
